answers.question: Business and size?
answers.answer: Furniture maker selling to retailers, revenue about $4.2M a year, 12% net margin (last year's accounts).

answers.question: Payment terms and stock?
answers.answer: Customers pay on 60-day terms, many late. We pay suppliers in 30 days. We carry about three months of timber stock.

answers.question: What has happened?
answers.answer: We hit the overdraft limit twice this quarter.

answers.question: What can the AI reach?
answers.answer: QuickBooks Online MCP read-only, bank statements as CSV.

answers.question: Target?
answers.answer: A cash buffer that never drops below $150,000 within six months.

answers.question: What must not happen?
answers.answer: Cannot lose the two biggest retail customers.

answers.question: Data home and decision maker?
answers.answer: A Google Sheet. The owner decides with the accountant.

answers.question: What is unknown?
answers.answer: How late customers really pay on average.

research.approach: Practitioners treat a profitable business running short of cash as a timing problem. They start from a reconciled opening cash balance, build a direct-method rolling 13-week forecast from receipts and payments rather than profit, and base collections on how each customer really pays, not on stated terms. They set a minimum cash line first, run more than one scenario, review forecast against actual every week, and then pull the cash levers in order: collections, stock buying, supplier timing and financing, with early moves inside four weeks and structural moves after that. Collections follow a dated escalation that protects key relationships.

steps.name: Reconcile opening cash and the ledgers behind the forecast
steps.why: Every forecast week depends on a correct opening balance, and receivables must tie to the ledger before they are treated as future cash.

steps.name: Measure how each customer really pays
steps.why: Collections should rest on observed payment history by customer, not the 60-day terms; the owner does not know the average.

steps.name: Find where profit turns into cash too late
steps.why: Terms of 60 days in, 30 days out and months of timber stock explain a gap that the profit and loss does not show.

steps.name: Build a direct-method forecast with a minimum cash line and scenarios
steps.why: A weekly receipts and payments forecast with a downside case shows when and by how much cash would fall below the floor.

steps.name: Rank the cash levers and choose
steps.why: Collections, stock buying, supplier timing and financing free different amounts of cash at different cost and risk.

steps.name: Run a dated, relationship-aware collections plan
steps.why: Early reminders and senior-level contact recover cash faster; key accounts need a personal approach.

steps.name: Buy timber to a target cover
steps.why: Stock above target cover is cash on the shelf; the next orders can be smaller.

steps.name: Agree supplier timing and financing before a breach
steps.why: Structural moves take weeks, and lenders and suppliers should be spoken to early.

steps.name: Review forecast against actual every week and roll forward
steps.why: Replacing the finished week with actuals and re-forecasting catches slips while there is still time to act.

pitfalls.text: Assuming optimistic collection timing instead of how customers actually pay.
Treating receivables as cash, or starting from an opening balance that is not reconciled.
Relying on a single scenario and forgetting irregular outflows such as taxes and annual premiums.
Building the forecast only during a crisis and not updating it weekly.
Early-payment discounts that cost more than the cash they free: 2/10 net 30 is roughly 37% annualised.
Chasing a key customer like any other, or looking only at average days outstanding and missing a few severely late accounts.

stages.name: Pin down the problem
stages.goal: Turn the owner's words into a measured cash problem, a $150,000 floor, limits and the data we can reach. Writes BRIEF.md.

stages.name: Pull cash, receivables, payables and stock
stages.goal: Collect twelve months of bank, invoice and bill history and the stock figures into the Google Sheet, with totals checked against the source.

outputs.name: Paid invoices with days to pay

checks.name: Bank, invoice and bill totals match QuickBooks and the CSV statements for the same dates
Covers twelve months, or the shorter period is stated
Anything not available is named as unknown, not estimated

stages.name: Check the opening cash and the ledgers
stages.goal: Reconcile the bank CSVs to QuickBooks balances, tie receivables ageing to the control account, and find unapplied payments, credit notes and duplicates before any forecast uses them.

checks.name: The opening balance on each account agrees to the bank statement, or the gap is itemised
Receivables and payables ageing total equals the ledger control account
Unapplied payments and credit notes are listed so overdue balances are not overstated
Ends with CHECKED, LIMITED or UNRELIABLE and what that means for the forecast

stages.name: Find where profit turns into cash too late
stages.goal: Measure days-to-pay by customer against the 60-day terms, the share of overdue money held by the two biggest customers, stock cover and the gap to 30-day supplier terms. Test each hypothesis.

checks.name: Average and spread of days to pay are computed from paid invoices, by customer, and the owner's unknown is replaced by a measured figure or stays unknown
Every hypothesis is marked SUPPORTED, REFUTED or UNKNOWN with evidence
The two biggest customers' share of receivables and of overdue balances is stated
Owner-reported numbers are labelled as reports

stages.name: Forecast weekly cash for six months
stages.goal: Build the direct-method weekly forecast from the checked opening cash, observed payment behaviour, dated outflows and stock buying, with a $150,000 line and a downside case where customers pay a week later.

checks.name: Built from receipts and payments by week, not from profit
Names the first week and size of any shortfall below $150,000 and below the overdraft limit
At least a base case and a downside with later customer payments
Tax, payroll and annual outflows are included with dates
The opening balance links to the checked figure in the opening cash check

stages.name: Rank the cash moves
stages.goal: Turn the findings into ranked moves, each with cash freed by week, cost, risk to the two biggest customers, effort and how it will be measured.

checks.name: Every move cites the finding it rests on
Every move has cash freed by week, cost, risk, effort and how it will be measured
The chosen combination keeps the downside case above $150,000, or says by how much it falls short
Any early-payment discount is priced as an annual cost

stages.name: Owner and accountant choose
stages.goal: The owner and accountant pick the moves. Ask why when a top move is passed over and record it.

checks.name: Chosen and passed-over moves are recorded with reasons
Any step involving the two biggest customers is explicitly approved or excluded

stages.name: Draft the collections plan and reminders
stages.goal: Rank overdue invoices by age and size, draft a dated reminder sequence for ordinary accounts and a personal approach for the two biggest customers.

checks.name: Each draft states the invoice, amount and due date, checked against QuickBooks
The two biggest customers have no automatic reminders, only talking points for the owner
Invoices with a dispute or unapplied payment are excluded from chasing
No threat or claim the owner has not approved

stages.name: Plan timber buying to a target cover
stages.goal: Set target cover from usage and supplier lead time, show cash tied above it, and schedule smaller or later purchase orders.

checks.name: Target cover is based on usage and lead time, and cash above target is stated
The plan states what stock level would stop orders being filled
Purchase changes are carried into the forecast

stages.name: Draft supplier terms and facility proposals
stages.goal: Prepare the supplier timing requests and a conversation with the bank about the overdraft or a line of credit, with the cost of each shown.

checks.name: Each request shows what it costs us and what it frees by week
Nothing offers a guarantee, security or new term the owner has not approved
Each is framed for a call or letter the owner sends

stages.name: Set up the weekly rolling forecast sheet
stages.goal: Turn the forecast into a rolling sheet with the $150,000 line, an alert for any week below it and a weekly update routine, including the chosen moves. One review for the owner and accountant: the forecast, the stock buying schedule and the chosen moves side by side. Reminders and supplier or bank requests are seen again one at a time when they are sent.

checks.name: Dropping a finished week and adding a new week is described step by step
Each input has an owner and a day of the week
Any week below $150,000 or within the overdraft margin is flagged

stages.name: Send approved messages and agree terms
stages.goal: The owner sends each approved reminder, makes each approved call and asks for each approved term change. The AI logs what was sent and what was promised.

outputs.name: Action log with promises to pay

checks.name: Each message or request has the owner's recorded approval before it goes
Promised payment dates are logged and carried into the forecast as promises, not cash
Contact with the two biggest customers is by the owner, in person or by phone

stages.name: Read forecast against actual every week
stages.goal: Compare actual closing cash and receipts with the forecast each week, track the lowest balance against $150,000 and days-to-pay, and flag breaches four weeks ahead.

checks.name: Actuals come from the bank, not from the forecast sheet
Overdraft use and the status of the two biggest customers are reported every week
No verdict on the six-month floor is given before the weeks have passed
Forecast error is shown by line so the biggest misses are fixed first

stages.name: Keep what we learned
stages.goal: Save measured payment behaviour, which moves worked and the rules for the forecast and the weekly review, and plan the next round.

checks.name: Each proposed rule says whether it holds for this job, this business or the playbook
The next round names the biggest remaining gap to the floor

hypotheses.statement: Customers pay materially later than the 60-day terms, and that gap is the main cause of the shortfalls.
hypotheses.test: Days from invoice date to paid date for 12 months of paid invoices, by customer and overall; compare with the 60 days.
hypotheses.confirm_if: Average or typical days to pay is clearly beyond 60 and the late invoices are most of the open balance.
hypotheses.refute_if: Most invoices are paid by day 60 and open balances are not mostly overdue.

hypotheses.statement: The two biggest customers hold most of the overdue money, so the fix is relationship-led rather than a general chase.
hypotheses.test: Share of receivables and of overdue balances by customer.
hypotheses.confirm_if: The two biggest customers hold a large share of the overdue balance.
hypotheses.refute_if: Overdue money is spread across many customers.

hypotheses.statement: Three months of timber stock is more than lead time and usage require, so cash sits on the shelf.
hypotheses.test: Stock value against monthly usage and supplier lead time, by timber type.
hypotheses.confirm_if: Cover is well above lead time plus a safety margin for most of the value.
hypotheses.refute_if: Cover is close to lead time, or long lead times justify it.

hypotheses.statement: Paying suppliers at 30 days while customers pay at 60 or later forces the overdraft to fund the gap.
hypotheses.test: Weekly forecast: do shortfalls follow clusters of supplier payments ahead of receipts?
hypotheses.confirm_if: Shortfall weeks follow bill payments that precede the related receipts.
hypotheses.refute_if: Shortfalls follow other lumps such as tax or payroll.

hypotheses.statement: One-off outflows (tax, payroll peaks, annual premiums, loan repayments) caused the two overdraft hits.
hypotheses.test: List dated outflows in the weeks before each overdraft hit and compare with a normal week.
hypotheses.confirm_if: A large dated outflow lands in the week of each hit.
hypotheses.refute_if: Normal weekly flows alone breached the limit.

hypotheses.statement: Unapplied payments or credit notes make the receivables look more overdue than they are.
hypotheses.test: List unapplied payments, credits and disputed invoices against open balances.
hypotheses.confirm_if: Unapplied items are a meaningful share of the overdue balance.

measurement.window: Every week for six months; the floor is judged on actual weekly closing balances from the bank.
measurement.min_volume: At least 13 weekly forecast-versus-actual comparisons before judging forecast accuracy; at least 12 months of paid invoices before treating days-to-pay as typical.
measurement.stop_rule: Escalate to the owner and accountant the same week if the forecast shows cash below $150,000 within four weeks or the overdraft is touched, and stop any step that puts one of the two biggest customers at risk.
